```{r setup, include = FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tmap)

#course data (read once for the whole page)
ch_rainfall <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1wYLHVVsemxQVjsdsmSzV9m0G6eLR_YK4", show_col_types = FALSE)
rdu_jan <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1ABpiu5ABzAo-WXbYBp9LWgN8-lHuFQR9", show_col_types = FALSE)
pm_nc <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=19Axv5_bv7p4LbDWNDs4TmdFi3gfYeNXc", show_col_types = FALSE)

#numbers quoted in the text below come from here, so they stay right if the data changes
fmt <- function(x, d = 3) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = d)
n_rain_rows <- nrow(ch_rainfall)
n_rain_dates <- n_distinct(ch_rainfall$date)
rain_years <- range(lubridate::year(ch_rainfall$date))
jan_years <- range(lubridate::year(rdu_jan$date))
```

::: {.plan}
- **Part 1 · about 15 min.** Read the walkthrough and run the code with your partner.
- **Part 2 · about 25 min.** Split up. Partner A uses the binomial and Partner B uses the normal model, both on bad-air days in Charlotte.
- **Part 3 · about 10 min.** Combine your numbers to answer one joint question, and write it on an index card.
:::

## Part 1 · Walkthrough {#walkthrough}

Run each chunk in your own .Rmd. You will reuse this code in Part 2.

### Step 1 · Load the data

::: {.why}
Daily rainfall in Chapel Hill (`r rain_years[1]` to `r rain_years[2]`, from the [NC State Climate Office](https://products.climate.ncsu.edu/data/)) and daily January highs at RDU airport (`r jan_years[1]` to `r jan_years[2]`, from the [Iowa Environmental Mesonet](https://mesonet.agron.iastate.edu/request/download.phtml)).
:::

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(sf)
library(tmap)

#daily rainfall in Chapel Hill
ch_rainfall <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1wYLHVVsemxQVjsdsmSzV9m0G6eLR_YK4")

#daily January high temperatures at RDU
rdu_jan <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=1ABpiu5ABzAo-WXbYBp9LWgN8-lHuFQR9")
```

### Step 2 · Make one row per day

::: {.why}
Probability counts days, so each row must be one day. The rainfall file has `r format(n_rain_rows, big.mark = ",")` rows but only `r format(n_rain_dates, big.mark = ",")` distinct dates. We keep one row per date and count the day as rainy if either record shows rain.
:::

```{r}
#one row per date, keeping the larger rainfall value
ch_daily <- ch_rainfall |>
  group_by(date) |>
  summarise(prec_in = max(prec_in))

#flag rainy days (1 = any rain, 0 = none)
ch_daily <- ch_daily |> mutate(rain = ifelse(prec_in > 0, 1, 0))
```

### Step 3 · Empirical probability

::: {.why}
**P(E) = f / n**: the number of days the event happened divided by the number of days observed.
:::

```{r}
#share of days with any rain
p_rain <- sum(ch_daily$rain) / nrow(ch_daily)
p_rain
```

### Step 4 · Binomial distribution

::: {.why}
The binomial counts "successes" in a fixed number of trials, each with the same probability. Rain isn't really independent from day to day, so treat this as a simplifying model.
:::

```{r}
#probability of 0 through 10 rainy days in 10 days
probability_days <- tibble(
  num_days = 0:10,
  probability = dbinom(x = 0:10, size = 10, prob = p_rain)
)

ggplot(probability_days, aes(x = num_days, y = probability)) +
  geom_col() +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:10)
```

```{r, include = FALSE}
most_likely <- probability_days |> slice_max(probability)
```

`pbinom(q, size, p)` gives the probability of **q or fewer**, so translate the question's wording first:

| Question says | Which outcomes | Code | Answer |
|---|---|---|---|
| most likely number | the tallest bar | `slice_max(probability_days, probability)` | `r most_likely$num_days` days (`r fmt(most_likely$probability)`) |
| 3 days or fewer | 0 to 3 | `pbinom(3, 10, p_rain)` | `r fmt(pbinom(3, 10, p_rain))` |
| more than 3 days | 4 to 10 | `1 - pbinom(3, 10, p_rain)` | `r fmt(1 - pbinom(3, 10, p_rain))` |
| at least 3 days | 3 to 10 | `1 - pbinom(2, 10, p_rain)` | `r fmt(1 - pbinom(2, 10, p_rain))` |

### Step 5 · Normal distribution

::: {.why}
A continuous variable can be modelled with a normal curve built from its mean and standard deviation. `pnorm()` gives the share *below* a value, so subtract from 1 for "above".
:::

```{r}
jan_mean <- mean(rdu_jan$max_temp)
jan_sd <- sd(rdu_jan$max_temp)

#normal model: probability of a high of 60 or above
1 - pnorm(60, mean = jan_mean, sd = jan_sd)

#empirical check: share of observed days at 60 or above
mean(rdu_jan$max_temp >= 60)

#histogram with the normal curve on top
ggplot(rdu_jan, aes(x = max_temp)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 4, boundary = 0) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = jan_mean, sd = jan_sd)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 60, linetype = "dashed")
```

::: {.reading}
The model says `r round(100 * (1 - pnorm(60, jan_mean, jan_sd)))`% of January days reach 60°F; the record says `r round(100 * mean(rdu_jan$max_temp >= 60))`%. Compare the model with the data before trusting it, especially in the tails.
:::

## Part 2 · Partner practice {#partner-practice}

Both partners use daily PM2.5 estimates for 300 North Carolina census tracts, 2016 to 2020, from the [CDC Environmental Public Health Tracking Network](https://ephtracking.cdc.gov/). Each row is one day in one tract. A **bad-air day** is a day with PM2.5 above 9.0 µg/m³, the EPA "moderate" line since 2024. The step to reuse is in parentheses.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#daily PM2.5 by census tract, 2016-2020 (both partners)
pm_nc <- read_csv("https://drive.google.com/uc?export=download&id=19Axv5_bv7p4LbDWNDs4TmdFi3gfYeNXc")
```

:::: {.partners}
::: {.partner .partner-a}
### Partner A · Binomial

1. Flag bad-air days, then find the empirical probability of a bad-air day for every tract by grouping on `lat` and `lon`. *(Step 3)*
2. Map those probabilities with `st_as_sf(coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)`. Longitude goes first.
3. For the tract at `lat` 35.142, `lon` -80.956 (southwest Charlotte), find the most likely number of bad-air days in a 30-day month. *(Step 4)*
4. Find the probability of **more than 15** bad-air days in a 30-day month for that tract. *(Step 4)*

**Bring to Part 3:** the tract's daily probability and your answer to item 4.
:::

::: {.partner .partner-b}
### Partner B · Normal model

1. Keep only the southwest Charlotte tract: `filter(round(lat, 3) == 35.142, round(lon, 3) == -80.956)`.
2. Find the mean and standard deviation of its daily PM2.5. *(Step 5)*
3. Use the normal model to find the probability that a day is above 9.0 µg/m³, and compare it with the empirical share of days above 9.0. *(Step 5)*
4. Plot a histogram of daily PM2.5 with the normal curve on top. *(Step 5)*

**Bring to Part 3:** the normal-model probability and one sentence on how well the curve fits.
:::
::::

## Part 3 · Together {#together}

1. Partner A runs Partner B's normal-model probability through the binomial: the chance of **more than 15** bad-air days in 30.
2. Partner B explains to Partner A why the two daily probabilities differ, using the histogram.
3. Decide together which estimate the county health department should use, and why.

| Daily probability from | Probability per day | P(more than 15 days in 30) |
|---|---|---|
| Empirical (Partner A) | | |
| Normal model (Partner B) | | |

::: {.deliver}
**Index card, one per pair.** Both names, the four numbers from the table, and your two or three sentences. Hand it in on your way out.
:::

## Answer key {#answer-key .answer-key}

```{r key-values, include = FALSE}
#Partner A
pm_prob <- pm_nc |>
  mutate(bad_air = ifelse(pm_val > 9, 1, 0)) |>
  group_by(lat, lon) |>
  summarise(p_bad_air = sum(bad_air) / n(), .groups = "drop")
tract <- pm_prob |> filter(round(lat, 3) == 35.142, round(lon, 3) == -80.956)
p_emp <- tract$p_bad_air
mode_emp <- which.max(dbinom(0:30, 30, p_emp)) - 1
more15_emp <- 1 - pbinom(15, 30, p_emp)
top_tract <- pm_prob |> slice_max(p_bad_air, n = 1, with_ties = FALSE)

#Partner B
charlotte <- pm_nc |> filter(round(lat, 3) == 35.142, round(lon, 3) == -80.956)
pm_mean <- mean(charlotte$pm_val)
pm_sd <- sd(charlotte$pm_val)
p_norm <- 1 - pnorm(9, mean = pm_mean, sd = pm_sd)
more15_norm <- 1 - pbinom(15, 30, p_norm)
```

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| A: tracts mapped | `r nrow(pm_prob)` |
| A: chance of a bad-air day, lowest to highest tract | `r fmt(min(pm_prob$p_bad_air))` to `r fmt(max(pm_prob$p_bad_air))` |
| A: southwest Charlotte, empirical daily probability | `r fmt(p_emp)` |
| A: most likely number of bad-air days in 30 | `r mode_emp` |
| A: P(more than 15 in 30), empirical | `r fmt(more15_emp)` |
| B: mean and sd of daily PM2.5 | `r fmt(pm_mean, 2)` and `r fmt(pm_sd, 2)` µg/m³ |
| B: normal-model daily probability | `r fmt(p_norm)` |
| Joint: P(more than 15 in 30), normal model | `r fmt(more15_norm)` |

**What a good card says.** Daily PM2.5 is right-skewed: most days sit a little below the mean and a few very smoky days pull the mean up. The normal curve is symmetric, so it puts too many days above 9.0 (`r fmt(p_norm)` vs `r fmt(p_emp)`), and that small gap grows to `r fmt(more15_norm)` vs `r fmt(more15_emp)` for more than 15 bad-air days in a month. The empirical estimate is the better one to use here.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
#### Partner A: binomial ####
#A1: flag bad-air days and find the empirical probability for every tract (Step 3)
pm_prob <- pm_nc |>
  mutate(bad_air = ifelse(pm_val > 9, 1, 0)) |>
  group_by(lat, lon) |>
  summarise(p_bad_air = sum(bad_air) / n())

#A2: map it (longitude goes first)
pm_prob_sf <- st_as_sf(pm_prob, coords = c("lon", "lat"), crs = 4326)
tm_shape(pm_prob_sf) +
  tm_dots(fill = "p_bad_air", size = 0.3,
          fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "P(bad-air day)"))

#A3: most likely number of bad-air days in 30 for southwest Charlotte (Step 4)
p_charlotte <- pm_prob |>
  filter(round(lat, 3) == 35.142, round(lon, 3) == -80.956) |>
  pull(p_bad_air)
bad_air_days <- tibble(num_days = 0:30,
                       probability = dbinom(0:30, size = 30, prob = p_charlotte))
bad_air_days |> slice_max(probability)

#A4: probability of MORE THAN 15 bad-air days in 30 (Step 4)
1 - pbinom(15, size = 30, prob = p_charlotte)

#### Partner B: normal model ####
#B1: keep the southwest Charlotte tract
charlotte <- pm_nc |> filter(round(lat, 3) == 35.142, round(lon, 3) == -80.956)

#B2: mean and standard deviation (Step 5)
pm_mean <- mean(charlotte$pm_val)
pm_sd <- sd(charlotte$pm_val)

#B3: normal-model probability of a day above 9.0, and the empirical check
1 - pnorm(9, mean = pm_mean, sd = pm_sd)
mean(charlotte$pm_val > 9)

#B4: histogram with the normal curve
ggplot(charlotte, aes(x = pm_val)) +
  geom_histogram(aes(y = after_stat(density)), binwidth = 1, boundary = 0) +
  stat_function(fun = dnorm, args = list(mean = pm_mean, sd = pm_sd)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 9, linetype = "dashed")

#### Part 3: together ####
p_normal <- 1 - pnorm(9, mean = pm_mean, sd = pm_sd)
1 - pbinom(15, size = 30, prob = p_normal)
```
